Fluid mechanics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 119k Articles: 2k
Fluid mechanics studies the motion and forces of liquids and gases. Its central simplification is the continuum approximation: replace individual molecules by bulk properties defined at every position and time. The averaging region must contain many molecules while remaining small compared with the distances over which those properties vary. A fluid element is such a small material parcel, rather than a single molecule. This connects fluid mechanics to continuum mechanics and makes calculus useful for describing flow. [ref]
Three basic fields are the velocity field u(x,t), the mass density ρ(x,t) and the pressure p(x,t). The first gives a parcel's instantaneous velocity; the second gives mass per unit volume. The pressure contributes an inward normal traction −pn across a surface with outward unit normal n. Thus pressure is a stress, measured in Pa=Nm−2, and may vary with position even in incompressible flow. Additional viscous stresses can act tangentially. [ref]
The guiding questions are what must be conserved and which forces matter. Mass conservation constrains the velocity field; momentum conservation determines its response to pressure gradients, viscosity and body forces. An incompressible flow model, a Reynolds number estimate and Bernoulli's principle answer different parts of a problem. Their appeal is that a few carefully stated assumptions can determine useful quantities before the entire velocity field is known.

Laminar flow

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Laminar flow is a regime of fluid flow in which the motion remains organized, with neighboring fluid parcels following smooth, coherent paths rather than the irregular interacting fluctuations characteristic of turbulence. In a straight pipe, the simplest example consists of coaxial layers sliding past one another. This describes the character of the motion, not a requirement that every parcel have the same velocity. Nor does it require steady flow: a smooth profile can evolve in time as viscosity transmits motion from a newly moving wall into a resting fluid. The unsteady wall-driven solution provides an explicit example. [ref]
The Reynolds pipe-and-dye experiment makes this distinction visible. A thin injected dye band can remain coherent in laminar flow, whereas irregular motion can fold it and carry dye across the pipe. However, molecular diffusion can spread dye even in laminar flow, and an inlet disturbance can move a coherent band without producing turbulence. A dye band is a streakline, not a measurement of the entire velocity field; in steady flow an ideal passive tracer's streakline coincides with a streamline. Reynolds explicitly distinguished a wandering band from one broken into eddies. [ref]
For a circular pipe of internal diameter D, define the mean axial velocity U using the volumetric flow rate Q and cross-sectional area A:
A=4πD2​,U=AQ​,ReD​=νUD​=μρUD​=πDν4Q​.
(1)
Here ρ is mass density, μ is dynamic viscosity and ν=μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity. This particular Reynolds number uses the diameter and mean velocity, not the radius or centreline velocity. Small Reynolds number generally favors laminar flow, but a single universal critical Reynolds number does not distinguish it from turbulence in all geometries and experiments. Even in a given pipe, inlet conditions and the magnitude of disturbances affect the observed onset. Reynolds demonstrated this dependence by deliberately inserting a wire coil. [ref]
The quantitative example above assumes steady flow, incompressible flow, a Newtonian fluid with constant dynamic viscosity, a straight horizontal circular pipe of radius R=D/2, stationary walls satisfying the no-slip boundary condition, and fully developed flow. The last assumption means that the axial velocity profile no longer changes downstream. A positive pressure drop Δp=pin​−pout​ over a developed length L gives the Hagen-Poiseuille equation:
u(r)=4μLΔp​(R2−r2)=2U(1−R2r2​),Q=∫0R​u(r)2πrdr=8μLπR4Δp​.
(2)
The velocity is zero at the wall and maximal at the centre. Averaging over the circular area, whose annuli have area 2πrdr, gives U=u(0)/2; averaging along one diameter would give a different answer. These assumptions produce a parabola, rather than every laminar flow having a parabolic profile. [ref]
As a stipulated calculation, take D=0.010m, U=0.10ms−1, ρ=1000kgm−3, μ=0.0010Pas and L=1.0m, and assume the developed laminar flow above. Then ν=10−6m2s−1, ReD​=1000, u(0)=0.20ms−1, Q=7.85×10−6m3s−1 (about 0.471Lmin−1), and Δp=32μLU/D2=32Pa. These are predictions from chosen parameters, not measurements or a claim that ReD​=1000 guarantees laminar flow in every apparatus.
The beauty of this example is that a spatially varying velocity field still gives an exact relation between two accessible measurements, pressure drop and volumetric flow rate. It predicts the hydraulic resistance Δp/Q=8μL/(πR4). Doubling the radius therefore multiplies Q by sixteen at fixed pressure drop, length and dynamic viscosity, provided the model remains applicable. This makes the laminar flow model useful for sizing narrow tubes or determining dynamic viscosity. It also explains why a persistent narrow dye band can be informative without implying that the fluid is moving as a uniform plug.

Reynolds pipe-and-dye experiment

Words: 732
Laminar flow OurBigBook.com
In his 1883 paper, Osborne Reynolds investigated how the character of pipe flow depends jointly on velocity, pipe diameter and viscosity. His final dye apparatus drew water from a large glass tank through a horizontal glass tube with a smooth trumpet-shaped entrance. A separate reservoir supplied strongly colored water just upstream of the entrance; a valve below the tank controlled the outflow. The glass tube was immersed in the tank, so its internal dye band could be watched. Reynolds repeated the trials with different tube diameters and water temperatures. [ref]
The volumetric flow rate was measured independently of the appearance of the dye. Reynolds timed a one-inch fall of the tank's water level, corresponding to a calibrated discharged volume. In modern notation, if this volume is V and the elapsed time is Δt, then Q=V/Δt and U=4V/(πD2Δt). He determined the glass tubes' internal diameters by filling them with water. For a uniform bore, a known filled length ℓ and measured water volume Vtube​ determine D=4Vtube​/(πℓ)​; checking bore uniformity matters because the same volume would only give an average cross-section in a tapered tube. Thermometers at different tank levels checked both the temperature and its uniformity. Reynolds compared the viscosity at different temperatures using Poiseuille's results and checked his own water by separate experiments of that type. Thus the Reynolds number estimate did not come from judging the dye band or from assuming that transition occurred at a preset value. [ref]
A practical repetition can instead collect a known outflow volume in a measuring vessel and time its collection, or weigh the collected water and divide its mass by mass density. Measure the internal diameter, rather than the external diameter, and obtain kinematic viscosity at the measured water temperature from independently established properties or a separate viscosity measurement. Record the dye appearance and observation position alongside Q, D, temperature and the resulting Reynolds number. These are alternative measurement procedures following Q=V/Δt, not additional historical claims about Reynolds' dye apparatus.
Begin with settled water and a small dye supply, then open the outlet valve in small steps. Reynolds saw a thin straight band at sufficiently low speeds. With a tank that had not fully settled, the band could wander while retaining its coherence. At higher discharge it could abruptly spread into the surrounding water downstream of the entrance. Short illumination by an electric spark resolved curls within what otherwise looked like a colored cloud. This connected the visible breakup with internal irregular motion rather than merely the appearance of an opaque pipe. [ref]
The controls are part of the result. Reynolds used a smooth entrance and let the tank rest to reduce inlet disturbances. He found that a heated tank could retain slow circulation as it cooled, so measuring one temperature was insufficient: thermal uniformity and residual motion also mattered. His wire-coil trial broke up the band below the previous onset speed, but he explicitly cautioned that once the dye was mixed he could not tell from that dye alone whether the motion became orderly again farther along the tube. In a repetition, keep the dye supply small enough to act approximately as a passive scalar, avoid a strong injection jet, and record the inlet condition and downstream observation distance. If also testing the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, allow the profile to develop and measure pressure drop between positions within the developed region; do not treat the entrance and outlet losses as part of its uniform pressure gradient. The dye experiment by itself does not establish fully developed flow. [ref]
The experiment's usefulness is that it compares a visible change in the motion with independently measured scales. Repeating it with several diameters and temperatures, while controlling disturbances, tests the organizing role of the Reynolds number. Its limitations are equally instructive: dye is a tracer of transport, diffusion still acts in laminar flow, and a local dye observation cannot by itself prove that turbulence persists throughout an arbitrarily long pipe.

A motivating experiment is to compare two independently observed quantities: the lift registered by a force balance, and the lift inferred from surface pressures. A low-speed wind tunnel holds the model fixed while air passes it at adjustable speed; a calibrated balance measures forces, while small flush holes on both surfaces connect by tubing to differential-pressure sensors referenced to p∞​. Iowa State's GA(W)-1 teaching model has 43 taps around a 101mm chord; its instructions give their coordinates and close the contour by repeating the first tap. A classroom comparison can combine this pressure-panel method with a balance on the same model; this is an experiment design, not a claim that those instructions report a combined measurement. Before turning on the wind, apply known positive and negative loads to the balance through its resolving centre; use mg for the known load from a mass. Record all balance channels during loading and unloading, including response to drag and torque loads, to detect cross coupling, hysteresis and zero drift. Record a wind-off tare at each model orientation so its weight does not become an aerodynamic lift reading. Inspect tubing for leaks and blocked taps, and wait for readings to settle before averaging: tubing can delay a pressure signal. This calibration principle is used in NASA's electronically scanned pressure systems, where several applied calibration pressures determine each sensor's response and repeated calibration tracks drift. A simple pressure standard can instead use a liquid-column height difference and the hydrostatic pressure law. [ref]

Record temperature and ambient pressure to determine mass density using the ideal gas law. At fixed q∞​, step the angle of attack, repeat selected settings, and sweep back down to check reproducibility. Record balance lift, each tap's mean pressure, and fluctuation sizes. Tunnel walls and model blockage alter the effective flow and require corrections; end plates or a model extending between walls approximate two-dimensional flow but do not guarantee it. Dynamic pressure is the bulk kinetic energy per unit volume associated with fluid motion at speed U in a specified reference frame:
q=21​ρU2,V21​mU2​=21​ρU2,Jm−3=Pa.
(7)
Here ρ=m/V is mass density. The word "pressure" identifies its units and its use as a pressure scale; q is not an extra isotropic stress to add to the local static pressure in every surface traction. A stationary fluid can have large static pressure with q=0. Conversely, knowing U and ρ fixes q without fixing static pressure. The definition remains useful in viscous fluid flow and compressible flow, even when the simplest Bernoulli equation is inapplicable. [ref]
For stipulated mass density ρ∞​=1.20kgm−3 and reference speed U∞​=20ms−1, q∞​=240Pa. At 40ms−1 with the same mass density, q∞​=960Pa. This quadratic scaling makes dynamic pressure a useful normalization for the lift coefficient, drag coefficient and pressure coefficient; it predicts four times a particular force only if its corresponding coefficient remains unchanged.
The connection with stagnation pressure requires hypotheses. For steady flow, constant mass density, inviscid flow, and gravity as the only body force, the Bernoulli equation gives, along one streamline,
p+21​ρU2+ρgz=B.
(8)
Here p is static pressure, g is gravitational acceleration, and z is height. Bring that flow to rest without losses at the same height and the limiting static pressure is the stagnation pressure p0​:
p0​=p+q,p0​−p=21​ρU2.
(9)
There must be no intervening pump supplying work or other energy input. Constancy along one streamline does not assert equal B on all streamlines; irrotational flow in a connected region supplies that additional conclusion. Changing height requires retaining ρgz. In compressible flow the stopping pressure difference generally differs from ρU2/2, and viscous dissipation can reduce recovered stagnation pressure. [ref]
A Pitot-static tube turns this relation into a measurement: its upstream-facing opening senses stagnation pressure, while separate side openings sample static pressure. Connect these to the positive and negative ports of a differential pressure transducer or manometer. Under the hypotheses above, the measured difference Δp gives
U=ρ2Δp​​.
(10)
Thus the stipulated 240Pa and 1.20kgm−3 imply 20ms−1, not an independently measured speed. Align the probe with the incoming flow and keep its passages clear: blockage and pinched tubing invalidate the comparison. At very low speed, the difference can be smaller than instrument error; at high Mach number, compressibility and possibly a shock wave require a different reduction. [ref]

The manufacturer's Series 475 Handheld Digital Manometer: Specifications - Installation and Operating Instructions by Dwyer Instruments, Inc. directs the user to vent both ports to the atmosphere before zeroing. Its stated accuracy is a fraction of full scale, not of the reading, and depends on instrument temperature. Select a suitable range and record the instrument variant and units; the manual covers several ranges.[ref]
An independent physical check can use a liquid-column manometer: apply a stable pressure difference to both instruments and compare the digital reading with the hydrostatic pressure inferred from the vertical level difference. Known mass densities, measured height and gravitational acceleration set the comparison scale. Check several differences across the working range and reverse the port connections to check the sign. This is a proposed independent check, not a claim that the cited teaching experiment performed a full instrument calibration. Recheck zero after reconnecting the sealed tubing; a zero adjustment alone cannot detect a blocked passage or an incorrect scale.

For stipulated p∞​=101325Pa absolute and q∞​=240Pa, Cp​=−3 gives p=100605Pa absolute: a 720Pa deficit, not a negative absolute pressure. The first equation immediately gives the second after subtracting p∞​ and dividing by q∞​. Hence a lossless stagnation point has Cp​=1, U=U∞​ gives Cp​=0, and U=2U∞​ gives Cp​=−3. For a real stationary wall satisfying the no-slip boundary condition, the velocity is zero right at the wall; inserting that wall velocity in an inviscid flow formula would wrongly predict Cp​=1 everywhere. A thin boundary layer approximation instead relates the wall pressure to the outer-flow pressure and uses the outer velocity where the Bernoulli equation applies.

With θ measured from downstream, the front is at π and the rear at zero. Both ideal stagnation points have Cp​=1, while the sides at π/2 and 3π/2 have Cp​=−3. This exact model is a useful baseline for an experiment; its complete rearward pressure recovery is not a prediction for a separated real fluid wake.

The full fluid force also includes ∫Σ​σvisc​ndA from the viscous stress tensor, including tangential shear stress; pressure tapping does not measure that contribution.

Real viscosity, boundary layers and flow separation can prevent rearward pressure recovery and produce pressure drag. Thus the measured curve can test the model and estimate a pressure contribution without proving that total drag vanishes.

Its open-jet wind tunnel holds a rotatable 140mm cylinder with end plates and 36 one-millimetre pressure tappings at ten-degree intervals. A reference Pitot-static tube supplies p0∞​ and p∞​ to one digital manometer; a second connects a surface tap to its positive port and reference static pressure to its negative port. Record tap positions after rotation. Compare the two instruments and check spanwise uniformity; end plates do not guarantee two-dimensional flow. [ref]

Measure room absolute pressure and temperature if converting the reference difference to speed through the ideal gas law ρ=pabs​/(RT); use thermodynamic temperature in that equation. For force reconstruction, cover the complete contour and use numerical integration with the tap geometry. Finite tap spacing, unknown end effects, probe disturbance and fluctuations limit that reconstruction; tubes and instruments also average or delay changing pressures. Retain the signed raw readings, repeated readings and reference readings so that these limits can be assessed. An airfoil (British spelling: aerofoil) is the cross-sectional profile of a lifting surface, such as a wing or blade. Its chord is the straight segment from leading edge to trailing edge, with length c; its mean camber line runs midway between its upper and lower surfaces, and its thickness measures their separation. Camber is the departure of that mean line from the chord. The angle of attack describes the profile's orientation relative to the incoming flow. These independent choices let a designer alter the distribution of pressure, lift and drag, rather than simply enlarging the surface. [ref]
The distinction between an airfoil and a finite wing matters. A two-dimensional section model assumes no variation along span and predicts lift per unit span L′. A wing of span b has a spanwise distribution L′(z) and total lift L=∫−b/2b/2​L′(z)dz. Its tip flow and trailing vortices generate a downward induced velocity, called downwash, which changes the local flow seen by the sections. Thus one cannot generally multiply the isolated two-dimensional L′ by b. The wing aspect ratio b2/S measures its span relative to its reference area and helps characterize these three-dimensional effects. [ref]
For a thin section with small camber slopes and small angle of attack, thin airfoil theory predicts
cl​≃2π(α−αL=0​),dαdcl​​≃2π,
(18)
where both angles are in radians and αL=0​ is the zero-lift angle of attack. The model assumes two-dimensional, steady flow, incompressible flow, inviscid flow, an attached outer flow, and smooth departure at a sharp trailing edge (the Kutta condition). This last condition selects the circulation used by the Kutta–Joukowski theorem; with counterclockwise circulation Γ positive and U∞​=U∞​ex​, that theorem gives L′=−ρ∞​U∞​Γ for positive lift towards +ey​. The beauty is that a detailed velocity field collapses to a simple force law, while the geometry enters through αL=0​. [ref] [ref]
A symmetric airfoil has αL=0​=0 in this model: at α=4∘=π/45 the predicted lift coefficient is cl​≃0.439, and reversing α reverses lift. A stipulated cambered section with αL=0​=−2∘ instead predicts cl​≃0.219 at zero angle of attack. These are ideal calculations, not measurements or guarantees for a particular profile. Air parcels on the upper and lower surfaces have no obligation to arrive together at the trailing edge; the pressure and velocity field must satisfy the flow problem. A symmetric lifting section already makes an unequal-path-length explanation inadequate. [ref]
Real airfoils have a viscous boundary layer, even when inviscid flow approximates the outer motion. At sufficiently demanding incidence, flow separation can become extensive and the lift coefficient departs from its approximately linear law, reaches a maximum and may fall: this is aerodynamic stall. Lift does not generally vanish at aerodynamic stall. The onset depends on profile, Reynolds number, surface condition and motion history; 2π(α−αL=0​) predicts neither a universal stall angle nor post-stall behavior. The pressure/balance experiment in lift makes this limit observable by measuring changes in the surface pressure distribution alongside the total force. [ref]

Fluid

Words: 185
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A fluid is a material that flows under sustained shear stress and cannot maintain a static shear stress in its fluid state. Liquids and gases are the usual examples. A Newtonian fluid has deviatoric stress proportional to its rate-of-strain tensor, whereas more general fluid constitutive equations can be nonlinear or have memory. In a porous medium, the fluid occupies connected voids within a load-bearing solid framework. The important distinction is the response to a continuing tangential force: an ordinary elastic solid can settle into a fixed deformation, while an ordinary fluid continues to deform. A fluid can nevertheless be at rest when no unbalanced shear stress drives it. [ref]
For a worked example, place a Newtonian fluid between parallel plates separated by h=1mm, keep the lower plate fixed and move the upper one at U=0.10ms−1. With no-slip boundary conditions, steady flow, no imposed pressure gradient and negligible edge effects, Couette flow has u(y)=Uy/h. For dynamic viscosity μ=0.001Pas, the shear stress magnitude is
τ=μdydu​=μhU​=0.10Pa.
(19)
The velocity gradient describes neighbouring layers sliding at different speeds. Doubling U doubles the required shear stress; maintaining the same velocity keeps producing deformation, rather than fixing a final shape. This gives viscosity a concrete meaning: resistance to a rate of motion, not a prohibition on motion.

A pathline is useful for answering where a particular parcel goes and how long it takes, rather than merely which way the fluid is moving now. [ref]
For a concrete analytical model, take spatial coordinates x,y in metres, time t≥0 in seconds, and the spatially uniform but time-dependent velocity field
u(x,y,t)=(U,at),U=1 ms−1,a=1 ms−2.
(21)
Its numerical components in these units are (1,t). A fluid element starting at the origin at t0​=0 has the pathline
x(t)=Ut,y(t)=2at2​,y=2U2a​x2.
(22)
At t=1 s it is at (1,0.5) m; at t=2 s it is at (2,2) m. The parabola records earlier, shallower velocity directions as well as the final direction. Differentiating gives (x˙,y˙​)=(U,at) and acceleration (0,a), so this curved pathline needs no spatial variation of the velocity field. More generally the chain rule along a pathline gives df(X(t),t)/dt=∂t​f+u⋅∇f, the material derivative of a transported scalar field.
A motivating tracer demonstration appears in S. J. Kline's film notes: water passes through a contracting channel, and hydrogen bubbles mark a small element at a wire at time t0​. The illustrated element is shown again 4.7 s later, with its accumulated pathline superposed. Following that same marked element across successive film frames records a history; the entire bubble pattern in one frame has a different meaning. [ref]
For a modern version of the readout, use sparse small markers in a transparent water channel, illuminate the viewed plane, and keep an optical camera fixed with a ruler in that plane. Record timestamps and track the same isolated marker between frames; successive positions estimate its pathline and [X(t+Δt)−X(t)]/Δt estimates its velocity. A long exposure records a pathline segment but loses the timing within it, so its total length divided by exposure time gives only mean speed. These are proposed measurement steps based on Jean Hertzberg's teaching guidance, rather than additional measurements from Kline's film. Markers leaving the viewed plane, overlapping tracks and perspective can break particle identification; repeat with a thinner viewed slice and a lower marker concentration. [ref]

For parallel flow past a flat, impermeable wall translating uniformly with tangential velocity Uw​, write the fluid's tangential velocity as u and its relative tangential velocity as urel​=u−Uw​. Then
urel​=b∂n​u,b≥0,
(23)
where b is the slip length, also written ℓs​. The unit normal n points from the wall into the fluid, and ∂n​u=n⋅∇u is the normal derivative. The separate no-penetration boundary condition requires (u−Uw​)⋅n=0: tangential sliding does not allow flow through the wall.
The sign convention matters. In a channel 0<z<H, the lower wall has inward unit normal +ez​ and the upper wall has inward unit normal −ez​. If both walls obey the Navier slip boundary condition, their tangential velocities satisfy

(24)
Here the prime means the derivative with respect to z. Using +bH​u′(H) at the upper wall would reverse the friction law. The examples Couette flow with a slipping lower wall and planar Poiseuille flow with equal wall slip use different upper-wall boundary conditions.
This flat-wall formula is a local linear model. On a curved wall the Newtonian fluid stress tensor must supply the tangential traction; the normal derivative alone generally misses curvature terms. The author-written review by Lauga, Brenner and Stone states the full strain-based condition with the unit normal directed into the liquid. [ref]
The same review credits Navier's 1823 treatise with the linear slip law. Its history is a reminder that the no-slip boundary condition is an experimentally successful model, whose validity depends on the interface and scale. The history here follows that review rather than a new reading of Navier's original memoir. [ref]

There is no streamwise pressure gradient or body force. The Couette flow solution is

(27)
Here τ is the constant shear stress magnitude. The lower wall's Navier slip boundary condition holds exactly because bu′(0)=bU/(H+b)=u(0). At the top, u(H)=U is exactly the prescribed no-slip boundary condition; no finite upper-wall slip length is imposed in this example.
For a numerical example, stipulate H=10μm, b=2μm, U=1mms−1 and μ=10−3Pas. The bottom velocity is 0.167mms−1 and the shear stress is 0.0833Pa, compared with 0.100Pa when both plates obey the no-slip boundary condition. The extrapolated profile reaches zero at z=−2μm.
For fixed H, U and μ, b→0 recovers u=Uz/H. As b→∞, u→U throughout the gap and τ→0: the moving upper wall selects the limiting uniform velocity, while the lower wall approaches a stress-free boundary condition. The dynamic viscosity stays positive; the disappearing shear stress comes from the disappearing velocity gradient.
A short derivation uses unidirectional flow: the convective acceleration vanishes and the Navier-Stokes equation reduces to μu′′=0. Write u=Az+B. The bottom condition gives B=bA and the top condition gives A(H+b)=U.

The full volumetric flow rate for channel width W is Q=Wq when side-wall effects are negligible. Thus q has units m2s−1, while Q has units m3s−1. Denote the value at b=0 by q0​=GH3/(12μ).
The two wall checks expose the normal signs:

(29)
bu′(0)=2μGbH​=u(0),−bu′(H)=2μGbH​=u(H).
(30)
Both Navier slip boundary conditions therefore hold exactly. The two walls exert backward tangential tractions of magnitude GH/2 on the fluid. Increasing b at fixed G adds a uniform velocity offset, leaving the velocity gradient and wall shear stress unchanged. This differs from Couette flow with a slipping lower wall, where upper-wall velocity is fixed and shear stress decreases.

At fixed H, G>0 and μ, b→0 recovers ordinary planar Poiseuille flow. As b→∞, the velocity and q grow without bound in this model, although the varying part of the profile stays the same. At exactly zero tangential wall traction, no steady solution can balance this nonzero pressure gradient: u′(0)=u′(H)=0 conflicts with μ[u′(H)−u′(0)]=−GH. Unlimited enhancement is consequently not a prediction for a real channel; finite wall friction, finite driving capacity and the validity of the assumed steady flow must be assessed. At fixed finite q instead, G→0 and the profile approaches uniform velocity q/H.

Buoyancy (Fb​)

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Buoyancy is the resultant upward force exerted by a resting fluid on an immersed body in a downward gravitational field. The fluid pushes inward, perpendicular to each part of the body's surface. Because hydrostatic pressure increases with depth, the upward push from below exceeds the downward push from above. Opposite horizontal forces cancel; buoyancy is the remaining vertical force. A sinking body still receives this upward support. [ref]
More precisely, pressure p on a small surface of area dA with outward unit normal vector n exerts
dF=−pndA.
(37)
The minus sign says the force points into the body. On a cube, the top force points down, the bottom force points up, and the side forces cancel in pairs because opposite sides have the same pressure at each depth. This is a surface traction; gravity on the body itself is a separate body force. [ref]
For a computed example, stipulate resting water with constant mass density ρf​=1000 kgm−3 and uniform gravitational acceleration g=9.81 ms−2. A fully immersed cube has side L=0.10 m, top depth ht​=0.20 m and bottom depth hb​=0.30 m. Each horizontal face has area A=L2=0.010 m2, and its volume is V=L3=0.001 m3. Its top and bottom gauge pressures are
pg,t​=ρf​ght​=1962 Pa,pg,b​=ρf​ghb​=2943 Pa.
(38)
The corresponding forces relative to the common surface pressure are pg,t​A=19.62 N downward and pg,b​A=29.43 N upward. Therefore the net buoyancy is
Fb​=(pg,b​−pg,t​)A=9.81 N.
(39)
Using absolute pressures adds the same psurface​A to both face forces, leaving their difference unchanged. Zero gauge pressure at the surface does not mean zero absolute pressure. Increasing both depths by the same amount also leaves buoyancy unchanged in this constant-mass density model.
Archimedes' principle turns this calculation into a rule for bodies of any shape. It explains floating equilibrium and lets us infer an immersed body's volume from the difference between its force from gravity and the force needed to support it. In particular, buoyancy depends on the displaced volume and the surrounding mass density, whereas the body's own mass density decides how its force from gravity compares with that support.

Archimedes' principle (Fb​=ρf​gVdisplaced​)

Words: 632 Articles: 1
Buoyancy OurBigBook.com
Archimedes' principle states that buoyancy equals the downward gravitational weight, or weight, of the displaced fluid. In a resting fluid of constant mass density ρf​ under uniform gravitational acceleration g, its magnitude is
Fb​=ρf​gVdisplaced​.
(40)
Here Vdisplaced​ is the volume from which the body excludes the fluid: the whole external volume for a fully immersed solid body, and just the immersed volume for a partly immersed one. The body's own mass does not enter this buoyancy formula. [ref]
A short proof outline for a fully immersed body is to imagine replacing it by exactly the fluid it displaces. The surrounding hydrostatic pressure is unchanged. That replacement fluid is at rest, so its upward pressure force must balance its downward force from gravity. The original body receives the same inward pressure forces on the same closed surface, hence the same upward buoyancy.
Equivalently, let Ω be the displaced region, ∂Ω its closed surface and ez​ the upward unit direction. The divergence theorem, applied component by component to the surface integral, and hydrostatic pressure give
Fb​=−∫∂Ω​pndA=−∫Ω​∇pdV=ρf​gVdisplaced​ez​.
(41)
This also explains why horizontal forces cancel even for an irregular shape. A spatially constant surface pressure contributes zero to the closed-surface integral. If the mass density varies with depth, replace ρf​Vdisplaced​ by the mass ∫Ω​ρf​dV of the displaced fluid.
The closed-surface argument assumes that the fluid applies pressure over the entire boundary of a fully immersed body. A body sealing against a tank bottom may have no fluid beneath it; then the lower-face pressure force used in the proof is absent, and a supporting contact force must be treated separately. For partial immersion, the usual buoyancy formula assumes the exposed surface receives the common atmospheric pressure, neglects the much smaller buoyancy from the air, and neglects surface tension.
For the 0.10 m cube in the stipulated water, full immersion displaces 0.001 m3, so Fb​=1000×9.81×0.001=9.81 N. If its uniform mass density is 600 kgm−3, its mass is m=600×0.001=0.600 kg and its downward force from gravity is mg=5.886 N. To hold it fully immersed at rest requires an additional downward force
Fhold​=Fb​−mg=9.81−5.886=3.924 N.
(42)
On release from rest it initially moves upward; its eventual floating equilibrium has a smaller displaced volume. A same-size cube of uniform mass density 1200 kgm−3 has mass 1.200 kg and downward force from gravity 11.772 N. Full immersion still gives 9.81 N of buoyancy, leaving an initial net downward force of 11.772−9.81=1.962 N. Subsequent motion also involves drag.

A freely floating body at rest has no supporting contact or applied holding force. Neglecting surface tension and the buoyancy of air, its upward buoyancy balances its downward force from gravity:
Fb​=mg.
(43)

Vbody​Vdisplaced​​=ρf​ρbody​​.

Partial immersion is possible when ρbody​<ρf​. A nonuniform body uses its mean mass density m/Vbody​ instead; for a hollow body this volume must count the enclosed space that excludes water. This explains how the amount of displaced water can support a vessel whose walls alone are denser than water. [ref]

Neutral buoyancy (ρbody​=ρf​)

Words: 123
Buoyancy OurBigBook.com
Neutral buoyancy means a fully immersed body's upward buoyancy equals its downward force from gravity. For a body of fixed volume in a constant-mass density fluid under a uniform gravitational field, this occurs when its mean mass density equals the surrounding mass density. A 0.10 m cube of mass density 1000 kgm−3 in the stipulated water has mass 1.000 kg, so both forces are 9.81 N.
Ideally it can remain at rest at any depth for which it stays fully immersed and clear of boundaries. Raising or lowering it changes the absolute pressure, but neither its displaced volume nor the difference between the vertical pressure forces. There is therefore no vertical restoring force toward a preferred depth in this model. Neutral buoyancy is a vertical force balance, not a claim about resistance to tilting or about a compressible body whose volume changes with pressure.

For a sphere of radius a, the usual choice is the frontal area A=πa2. Choosing its entire surface area 4πa2 instead divides the reported drag coefficient by four for the same physical drag force. The vector formula makes the direction explicit: the drag force on the body opposes its motion relative to the fluid, and vanishes at U=0. For a general body, orientation and other flow conditions can affect the drag coefficient; treating it as a constant requires a regime in which that is an adequate approximation. [ref]
Compare two distinct models at a chosen relative speed U0​>0. A linear drag model has FD​(U)/FD​(U0​)=U/U0​, while a constant-coefficient quadratic drag model has FD​(U)/FD​(U0​)=(U/U0​)2. At U=2U0​ their drag force ratios are two and four respectively.
This distinction matters when estimating terminal velocity or trajectories such as descent from rest under quadratic drag: doubling relative speed increases the resistance much more strongly in the quadratic drag model. An approximately constant drag coefficient can occur in another Reynolds number regime; its use must be justified there. Conversely, substituting the creeping-flow sphere coefficient CD​=24/Red​ into FD​=21​ρU2ACD​ recovers linear drag, so writing this general formula does not make the resistance quadratic. Neither approximation should be extended across all Reynolds numbers.
The distinction already appears in the original investigation underlying the Stokes drag law, read on 9 December 1850: article 42 identifies resistance proportional to relative speed and distinguishes it from a contribution proportional to the square of relative speed. [ref]

Reynolds number (Re=ρUL/μ=UL/ν)

Words: 249

The Reynolds number Re=UL/ν compares inertial and viscous effects. Here U is a characteristic velocity, L a characteristic length, μ the dynamic viscosity, ρ the mass density, and ν=μ/ρ the kinematic viscosity. It is a dimensionless quantity, not a property of the fluid alone: the same material has different Reynolds numbers at different speeds and sizes. Specify the chosen scales when reporting it.
The comparison comes from the Navier-Stokes equation. For velocity variations on scale L, convective acceleration is of order U2/L, while the viscous term is of order νU/L2. Their ratio is UL/ν. Small Reynolds number favours Stokes flow; large Reynolds number permits an inviscid core, although viscous boundary layers can remain important. Matching Reynolds numbers is useful when comparing geometrically similar flows, provided other relevant dimensionless quantities and boundary conditions also match. [ref]
In the constriction example under incompressible flow, use the mean axial velocity and pipe diameter, L=D=2R. Taking ρ=1000kgm−3 and a stipulated dynamic viscosity μ=0.001Pas gives
Re1​=0.0011000(0.20)(0.020)​=4000,Re2​=0.0011000(0.80)(0.010)​=8000.
(66)
Halving the radius at fixed volumetric flow rate doubles this diameter-based Reynolds number, because mean velocity increases fourfold. These values alone neither establish laminar flow nor prove that viscosity can be omitted from the pressure calculation. Increasing μ to 0.10Pas with the same imposed flow gives 40 and 80, but strengthens viscous effects; small Reynolds number does not justify Bernoulli's principle.
The name recalls Osborne Reynolds's 1883 experimental investigation of water motion and resistance in pipes. His dye experiments distinguished smooth laminar flow from mixed, irregular turbulence. [ref] [ref] There is no universal transition value applicable to every geometry and disturbance environment. [ref]

Use vorticity to distinguish the local spin of a fluid element from the motion of its center along a pathline. Circular streamlines can occur both with and without vorticity: the two velocity fields below even have the same circulation around the unit circle.
For a continuously differentiable velocity field u=(ux​,uy​,uz​), vorticity is the curl vector
ω=∇×u=(∂y∂uz​​−∂z∂uy​​,∂z∂ux​​−∂x∂uz​​,∂x∂uy​​−∂y∂ux​​).

Each partial derivative divides velocity by distance, so vorticity has units s−1. In a planar velocity field independent of z, only ωz​=∂x​uy​−∂y​ux​ survives. Positive ωz​ points along +ez​: the right-hand rule associates it with counterclockwise spin viewed from positive z toward the plane. [ref]
The local rotational angular velocity is half the vorticity, Ωspin​=ω/2. To see the factor, split the velocity gradient Lij​=∂j​ui​ into its symmetric rate-of-strain tensor E=(L+LT)/2 and antisymmetric spin tensor W=(L−LT)/2. A nearby displacement δx has relative velocity Lδx; its rotational part satisfies Wδx=(ω/2)×δx. This is a proof outline of the local spin interpretation. The rate-of-strain tensor can also change the angle of a particular material line, so that line's angular velocity need not equal ω/2.
For solid-body rotation, u=(−Ωy,Ωx,0) gives ω=(0,0,2Ω) and Ωspin​=(0,0,Ω). Taking Ω=1 s−1, the vorticity is 2ez​ s−1, although the angular velocity is only 1ez​ s−1. For the potential line vortex, u=Keθ​/r, the planar curl is r−1∂r​(ruθ​)=r−1∂r​K=0 wherever r>0. Its circular pathlines therefore coexist with zero local spin.
This distinction makes vorticity useful for recognizing shear flow as well as swirling motion; taking the curl of the Euler equations also removes a pressure gradient and leads to the vorticity equation. A historical landmark is Hermann von Helmholtz's 1858 paper on fluid vortex motion, an early study devoted to vortex dynamics. [ref]

Streamline

Words: 487 Articles: 1
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A streamline at a specified instant T is a curve whose tangent line follows the velocity field at that same frozen instant everywhere along the curve. One convenient integral curve parameterization is
dsdγ​=u(γ(s),T),T fixed.
(78)
Here s is an auxiliary curve parameter, with units of seconds in this convention; advancing s does not advance physical time. Any regular reparameterization preserves the tangent geometry. Where ux​=0, a planar streamline satisfies dy/dx=uy​/ux​ evaluated at time T. At a stagnation point the velocity field has no direction; under the local Lipschitz condition of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, regular streamlines at the same time cannot cross. A streamline answers which directions fit together now, making it useful for describing local flow geometry. [ref]
In the analytical velocity field (U,at) introduced under pathline, the streamline through the origin at time T is
y=UaT​x.
(79)
At T=2 s this is y=2x when both coordinates are expressed in metres. At x=1 m its height is 2 m, whereas the earlier pathline of the origin's first released fluid element has height 0.5 m. Its instantaneous streamline at the final position (2,2) m is instead y−2 m=2(x−2 m): the pathline is tangent to that streamline at its current endpoint, although its recorded history does not lie along it.
The green streamline uses the velocity field at T=2 s throughout; the orange pathline uses times 0≤t≤2 s; the purple streakline uses different release times at the single observation time T=2 s. The grey arrows all show the instantaneous velocity direction at T. These are exact analytical curves with chosen units, not measured dye shapes.
In a steady flow in a fixed reference frame, a pathline and a streamline solve the same autonomous ordinary differential equation. Uniqueness makes each particle released from a fixed point follow the same integral curve, so its pathline, the streakline from that point and the streamline share one geometrical curve. Finite recording or release intervals usually show different segments of that curve; the comparison assumes particles stay in the domain and treats stationary fluid elements separately. Neither two-dimensionality nor incompressibility is needed for this coincidence. Steadiness is sufficient, but is not necessary: u(x,t)=g(t)v(x) with smooth g(t)>0 changes speed while preserving the same integral curves. In a general time-dependent velocity field, however, the three curves differ. Kline explains why continuous dye release in steady flow can therefore display streamlines. [ref]
For two-dimensional incompressible flow, the convention u=(∂y​ψ,−∂x​ψ) gives u⋅∇ψ=0, so regular streamlines are level sets of the stream function at each frozen time. In time-dependent incompressible flow, that does not force a pathline to stay on one numerical value of ψ: its material derivative is Dψ/Dt=∂t​ψ. The distinction is the difference between a geometric snapshot and a parcel's history.

A full annulus therefore admits local angle branches and a multivalued velocity potential, but no global single-valued velocity potential when K=0. The Bernoulli principle relates pressure, kinetic energy per unit volume and Newtonian gravitational potential along a streamline of steady flow with inviscid flow. For constant mass density, the Bernoulli equation gives p/ρ+u2/2+Φ constant along that streamline. Constancy across different streamlines requires further hypotheses, such as irrotational flow.
Precisely, suppose a fluid of constant positive mass density obeys the Euler equations for an inviscid fluid, its velocity field and pressure are steady, and the body force per unit mass is −∇Φ. Then

(92)
Every term has units of energy per unit mass. For a uniform gravitational field, Newtonian gravitational potential is Φ=gz, up to an additive constant. The pressure term represents work by surrounding fluid, so acceleration can exchange pressure work with kinetic energy. Dotting the steady Euler equations with u gives the displayed directional derivative: this is why constancy follows a streamline. [ref]
Continue the horizontal water constriction example from incompressible flow. Assume negligible viscous losses, steady flow and approximately uniform flow at both measurement sections, so the streamline speeds there equal the mean speeds 0.20 and 0.80ms−1. Equal height cancels the Newtonian gravitational potential terms. The ideal pressure drop is
p1​−p2​=2ρ​(U22​−U12​)=21000​(0.802−0.202)=300Pa.
(93)
This is the Venturi effect in its ideal limit: the gain in kinetic energy density is supplied by pressure work. Cambridge's treatment uses this relation to connect a measured pressure difference to volumetric flow rate. [ref]
The 300Pa result is conditional, rather than a prediction of the actual viscous pipe. Mass conservation fixes Q and the ratio of mean speeds even with viscosity, but nonuniform velocity profiles require an integrated energy balance, and wall friction dissipates mechanical energy. A pump would supply additional work. In particular, constant mean speed in a straight pipe does not imply constant pressure: Poiseuille flow needs a continuing pressure gradient to overcome viscosity. [ref]

Surface tension (γ)

Words: 4k Articles: 39
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Surface tension γ is the tensile force per unit length across a line drawn in a liquid interface. For a clean interface with isotropy, it has the same value in every tangential direction: each side pulls the other along the surface, perpendicular to the line. A straight segment of length ℓ therefore transmits a force of magnitude γℓ from one interface. Here we assume constant γ>0, with fixed temperature and composition. The same coefficient measures the reversible work required to create surface area:
Fone interface​=γℓ,dEs​=γdA,[γ]=Nm−1=Jm−2.
(99)
The equality of units follows from 1J=1Nm; the equality of the mechanical coefficients follows from the moving-rim argument below. [ref] [ref]
For a concrete example, take an ideal flat soap film spanning a rectangular wire frame with a straight sliding rim of length ℓ. Pull the rim outwards in the plane of the film, perpendicular to the rim. Each of the film's two liquid–gas interfaces pulls the rim back towards the film with force γℓ, so the outward holding force is F=2γℓ. The two faces are two interfaces, each with its own surface tension. With the assumed toy value γ=0.072Nm−1 and ℓ=20mm=0.020m, the required force is 2.88mN; one interface would contribute 1.44mN. This value of γ is a stipulated model parameter, rather than a measured value for a particular soap solution.
Why does an interface resist being enlarged? Its molecules have a different environment from those in the bulk liquid; changing that environment has an energy cost. In the constant-surface tension model, reducing surface area lowers surface energy. This connects an easily measured rim force to the shape of a droplet, the Young–Laplace equation for its pressure, and the restoring mechanism of capillary waves. It is useful because one coefficient links forces, energy and geometry. [ref]
The moving-rim argument also explains the factor of two without memorizing a special formula. An outward displacement dx creates surface area ℓdx on each face, hence dAtotal​=2ℓdx. Slow pulling without viscous dissipation requires work Fdx=γdAtotal​, giving F=2γℓ. For one interface, the same argument gives F=γℓ. A surface tension gradient instead produces Marangoni stress; the constant-γ assumption excludes that additional effect.

Surface energy (Es​=γA)

Words: 260
Surface tension OurBigBook.com
For a liquid interface with constant surface tension γ, the mechanical surface energy is the energy associated with its surface area A:
Es​=γA+C,Es​(A2​)−Es​(A1​)=γ(A2​−A1​).
(100)
The additive constant C does not affect the work needed to change surface area. For several interfaces with the same surface tension, A means their total surface area; the two faces of a thin soap film must both be counted. [ref]
With assumed γ=0.072Nm−1, creating 1cm2=10−4m2 of one interface requires 7.2μJ of reversible work. In the sliding-rim example illustrated under surface tension, moving a 20mm rim outwards by 1mm creates 4.0×10−5m2 across the two faces and requires 2.88μJ. Independently, multiplying its 2.88mN holding force by the displacement gives the same work.
This makes the preference for a round isolated droplet precise. At fixed volume V, the three-dimensional isoperimetric inequality gives
A3≥36πV2,
(101)
with equality for a sphere. Thus a sphere minimizes surface energy among sufficiently regular closed shapes enclosing the same volume, when surface tension is uniform and other energy contributions are negligible. This is an application of the isoperimetric inequality, rather than a proof of it. Walls, wetting, and gravity can change the shape by adding constraints or other energy contributions. [ref]
The differential rule dEs​=γdA integrates directly to Es​=γA+C because surface tension is constant. At fixed liquid volume, decreasing surface area can drive viscous fluid flow; the released surface energy can supply viscous dissipation. This mechanical bookkeeping is useful for predicting which deformations can release energy. If surface tension depends on temperature or composition, distinguish this mechanical area-work relation from the complete interfacial thermodynamic free energy and internal energy.

Young–Laplace equation (Δp=γκ)

Words: 468 Articles: 2
Surface tension OurBigBook.com
The Young–Laplace equation relates the pressure jump across a stationary interface to its curvature and surface tension. Choose a unit normal vector n pointing from the inside region to the outside region, and define κ=∇s​⋅n to be positive for a convex sphere. In mechanical equilibrium, with constant surface tension and no additional normal viscous stresses,
Δp=pin​−pout​=γκ=γ(k1​+k2​).
(107)
Here k1​,k2​ are the signed principal curvatures in this convention. Their sum is twice the corresponding signed mean curvature; stating the convention prevents a factor-of-two ambiguity. The Young–Laplace equation is a local normal stress balance for one interface. [ref]
A spherical liquid droplet of radius R in a gas has one interface, with k1​=k2​=1/R. An ideal thin soap bubble has two liquid–gas interfaces. Adding their pressure jumps gives
Δpdroplet​=R2γ​,Δpsoap bubble​≃R4γ​.
(108)
For the soap bubble, Δp now means the inner gas pressure minus the outer gas pressure. The second formula assumes equal surface tensions on both faces and film thickness negligible relative to R, so their radii can be identified. Retaining distinct radii gives 2γ/Rinner​+2γ/Router​. A gas bubble inside bulk liquid has only one interface and therefore uses 2γ/R. [ref]
With the assumed constant toy surface tension γ=0.072Nm−1, a droplet with R=1mm has excess pressure 144Pa; at R=0.5mm it has 288Pa. A thin soap bubble assigned the same γ and R=1mm has excess pressure 288Pa. These are differences from the surrounding pressure, rather than absolute pressures. Halving the radius doubles the capillary pressure; doubling the interface count also doubles it at fixed radius and surface tension.
The spherical case has a short work argument. A virtual increase in radius gives dV=4πR2dR and dA=8πRdR. At mechanical equilibrium, the net pressure work balances the increase in surface energy:
pressure workΔp4πR2dR​​=surface energy increaseγ8πRdR​​⟹Δp=R2γ​.
(109)
For a thin soap bubble, both interfaces gain approximately the same surface area, doubling the right-hand side and giving 4γ/R. This is a virtual work balance between neighboring spherical configurations, rather than an assumption that a fixed-volume droplet actually expands. The general Young–Laplace equation replaces the spherical area-to-volume ratio by local curvature, making geometry directly measurable through pressure.

Capillary wave

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Surface tension OurBigBook.com
A capillary wave is a wave along a fluid interface whose restoring stress is predominantly supplied by surface tension. A curved free surface requires a pressure jump by the Young–Laplace equation; increasing its corrugation also costs surface energy. In the ideal limit, inertia carries the interface through its flat position and the resulting oscillation propagates. When gravity also contributes appreciably, use the combined gravity-capillary wave model. Within the capillary wave regime, shortening a ripple makes it travel faster. [ref]
The laser-diffraction measurement of capillary waves below turns this mechanism into a test: set the frequency, measure the wavelength independently with light, and ask whether the dispersion relation follows. The theory is useful both for predicting how ripple wave packets separate and for inferring surface tension from their motion.

Gravity-capillary wave (ω2=gk+(γ/ρ)k3)

Words: 470
Capillary wave OurBigBook.com
A gravity-capillary wave has restoring contributions from both gravity and surface tension. Consider an initially resting, horizontally unbounded liquid layer of constant depth h, with uniform mass density ρ, incompressible flow, inviscid flow and irrotational flow. The upper gas exerts constant pressure and has negligible inertia. Assume a clean interface with constant surface tension γ: no surfactant stresses, imposed current or wind. The wave amplitude a must satisfy ka≪1 and a≪h, so linearized boundary conditions apply. Deep water means kh≫1, rather than a particular depth in metres. [ref]
Let z=0 be the undisturbed free surface, with liquid below it. Potential flow gives a velocity potential ϕ with u=∇ϕ, and incompressible flow gives the Laplace equation. The linearized kinematic boundary condition for a free-surface graph and the Unsteady Bernoulli equation, including gravity and the Young–Laplace equation, give
ϕxx​+ϕzz​=0(z<0),ηt​=ϕz​,ϕt​+gη−ργ​ηxx​=0(z=0).
(112)
Here η(x,t) is the interface displacement; the signed small-slope pressure jump is pliquid​−pgas​=−γηxx​. A wave crest has ηxx​<0, so its capillary pressure is positive. Choose a right-travelling Fourier mode of positive wavenumber k and angular frequency ω:
η=acos(kx−ωt),ϕ=kaω​ekzsin(kx−ωt).
(113)
The factor ekz decays into the deep liquid, satisfies the Laplace equation, and makes ϕz​=ηt​ at z=0. Substituting in the dynamic boundary condition leaves
−kaω2​+ga+ργ​k2a=0,ω2=gk+ργ​k3​.
(114)
This derivation displays the two restoring contributions with the same sign. Dimensional analysis also checks the result: γ/ρ has units m3s−2, so both gk and (γ/ρ)k3 have units s−2. [ref]
At finite depth, a flat impermeable bottom at z=−h requires ϕz​=0. Replacing ekz by the normalized vertical factor cosh(k(z+h))/cosh(kh) makes the surface ratio ϕz​/ϕ=ktanh(kh). Eliminating the mode amplitudes then gives
ω2=(gk+ργ​k3)tanh(kh).
(115)
Thus the same model supplies its own depth check: use the deep-water formula only when tanh(kh) is sufficiently close to one for the required accuracy. For example, kh=3 reduces ω by about 0.248% relative to deep water, while kh=1 reduces it by about 12.7%. These percentages are calculations from this factor. [ref]
In deep water the phase velocity magnitude follows a wave crest, while the group velocity magnitude follows the wave envelope of a narrow wave packet. Differentiating the positive-frequency dispersion relation gives
cp​=kω​=kg​+ργk​​,cg​=dkdω​=2gk+γk3/ρ​g+3γk2/ρ​,cp​cg​​=2(1+(kℓc​)2)1+3(kℓc​)2​.
(116)
For kℓc​≪1, the surface gravity wave limit has cg​≃cp​/2. For kℓc​≫1, the deep-water capillary-wave dispersion relation has cg​≃3cp​/2: a wave crest slips backward relative to the faster wave envelope, even while both advance. Neither speed is the oscillating fluid element's own velocity. [ref]
There is a particularly neat coincidence at the crossover. Differentiate cp2​=g/k+γk/ρ: its unique minimum is at kc​=ρg/γ​=1/ℓc​, exactly where the restoring terms are equal. Therefore
cp,min​=(ρ4gγ​)1/4,cg​(kc​)=cp​(kc​).
(117)
For the stipulated parameters in capillary length, the minimum is 0.231ms−1. At λ=3mm, direct substitution gives f=ω/(2π)≃131Hz, cp​≃0.394ms−1 and cg​≃0.580ms−1. This short wavelength is capillary dominated, but its group velocity is still slightly below the pure-capillary ratio 3cp​/2 because gravity has not vanished.

Laser-diffraction measurement of capillary waves

Words: 469
Capillary wave OurBigBook.com
Zhu, Miao, Xu and Cao's 2007 experiment drove a triangular metal frame electromagnetically with a sinusoidal generator. In a roughly 3cm-deep, temperature-regulated pool, it produced nearly plane capillary waves. A 632.8nm laser illuminated the surface obliquely; the moving ripples acted as a reflection diffraction grating. One split beam monitored laser stability, while a CCD recorded diffraction orders on a screen 6.76m away. An air-supported optical table reduced ambient vibration. [ref]
The frequency sweep was 100–290Hz in 10Hz steps, using distilled water and kerosene at 20∘C. For each setting they averaged at least three measurements of first-order spot separation. Known optical geometry and the grating equation yielded k=2π/λ; generator readings yielded ω=2πf. Agreement with the predicted log–log slope 3/2 tests the capillary law, and its intercept gives surface tension if mass density is known. The authors identify surface contamination as a major error source; noncontact optical detection reduces additional disturbance. [ref]
The optical measurement can be understood from the grating equation. Let λL​ be the laser wavelength, α the incident grazing angle above the mean surface, and βm​ the outgoing grazing angle of diffraction order m, with the sign of m chosen so that
λ(cosα−cosβm​)=mλL​.
(118)
Thus calibrated spot positions determine outgoing angles, which determine the ripple wavelength λ, independently of the mechanical dispersion relation. This optical geometry treats the surface as a reflection diffraction grating at the laser wavelength. [ref]
The inferred surface tension in the full deep-water model is
γ=ρk3ω2−gk​.
(119)
This formula makes useful experimental controls explicit. Measure mass density at the sample's temperature; check depth with kh; keep the driven wave amplitude small enough that ka≪1; and distinguish f from angular frequency ω. For the stipulated parameters, the 100–290Hz window corresponds to calculated wavelengths about 3.62–1.76mm and kh≃52–107 at h=30mm. Depth corrections are negligible here, but the gravity contribution is about 4.5%–1.1% of the capillary contribution. These are ideal predictions, not digitized results from the experiment.
Omitting gravity would infer γcap​=ρω2/k3=γ+ρg/k2, biasing surface tension upward. In the capillary limit, the differential estimate dγ/γ≃dρ/ρ+2dω/ω−3dk/k also shows why careful spot-spacing calibration matters. A clean surface and weak viscosity are modeling assumptions: appreciable damping, surfactant stresses or large wave amplitudes call for additional physics. The experiment tests the short-wave regime; its drive window does not establish the crossover or the long-wave surface gravity wave limit.

Gravity is the example used in hydrostatic pressure: a gravitational field g gives force per unit volume ρg, where ρ is the mass density. Surface pressure forces produce buoyancy on an immersed body, while its body force from gravity acts downward.

Incompressible flow (∇⋅u=0)

Words: 458 Articles: 4
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An incompressible flow preserves the volume of each moving fluid element. Its local condition is zero velocity divergence, ∇⋅u=0. Combined with mass conservation, it says that each parcel's mass density stays unchanged as it moves. This does not require every parcel to have the same mass density: an initially nonuniform distribution can be transported without compression. Nor does incompressibility require a constant velocity or constant pressure.
For positive mass density, the continuity equation makes the equivalence precise:
∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅(ρu)=0,DtDρ​+ρ∇⋅u=0,DtD​=∂t∂​+u⋅∇.
(138)
The material derivative follows a fluid element. Thus Dρ/Dt=0 if and only if the velocity field is a divergence-free vector field. The distinction between following a parcel and observing a fixed position prevents confusing incompressibility with an unchanging density field. [ref]
For a rigid pipe with impermeable walls, no leaks and steady flow, mass conservation at constant mass density implies a constant volumetric flow rate:
Q=∫A​u⋅ndA=AU,A1​U1​=A2​U2​.
(139)
Here n points downstream, A is the section's area and U is the mean normal velocity, not necessarily the centreline speed. No assumption of inviscid flow or a uniform velocity profile is needed. If unequal amounts entered and left a fixed segment, its mass would accumulate, contradicting steady flow.
For a worked example, take horizontal water flow with stipulated mass density 1000kgm−3, inlet radius R1​=0.010m, outlet radius R2​=0.005m and inlet mean velocity U1​=0.20ms−1. The circular areas give
Q=πR12​U1​=2π×10−5m3s−1,U2​=πR22​Q​=0.80ms−1.
(140)
The radius halves, the area falls to one quarter, and the mean velocity quadruples. The mass flow rate is ρQ=0.02πkgs−1. The same amount of water passes both sections each second; narrowing changes its speed rather than compressing it. The Reynolds number and Bernoulli's principle discussions use this same example to examine viscous effects and the additional assumptions needed to calculate pressure.

Streakline

Words: 682
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A streakline at observation time T is the set of present positions of all fluid elements that passed through one fixed release point a during a specified history of injection. For continuous release over τ0​≤τ≤T, solve a different initial value problem for each release time τ:
∂t∂X​(t;τ,a)=u(X(t;τ,a),t),X(τ;τ,a)=a,ST​={X(T;τ,a):τ0​≤τ≤T}.
(141)
Thus a pathline varies t for one particle; a streakline varies τ while holding T fixed. Interrupted release gives only the corresponding subsets of the streakline. A moving nozzle requires a time-dependent release position instead, so the standard fixed-point definition should not silently be applied to it. Continuous release makes streaklines easy to observe and useful for showing where material from one source has reached. [ref]
In the analytical velocity field (U,at) of pathline, a particle released at the origin at time τ follows
x(t;τ)=U(t−τ),y(t;τ)=2a​(t2−τ2),t≥τ.
(142)
Observe all particles together at time T, after continuous release from τ=0:
x=U(T−τ),y=2a​(T2−τ2),y=UaT​x−2U2a​x2,0≤x≤UT.
(143)
For U=1 ms−1, a=1 ms−2 and T=2 s, the streakline is the downward-curving parabola y=2x−x2/2 in metre coordinates. Releases at τ=0,1,2 s occupy (2,2), (1,1.5) and (0,0) m, respectively. At x=1 m, the streakline lies above the pathline y=x2/2 and below the origin's streamline y=2x. All particles nevertheless have the same present velocity (1,2) ms−1. The streakline slope dy/dx=aτ/U generally differs from the present velocity slope aT/U; they agree at the nozzle. The oldest particle is the downstream endpoint, which explains why the pathline and streakline meet there without being the same curve.
Each panel fixes one observation time. Coloured dots are the present positions of particles with the indicated release times; dashed pathlines show those particles' earlier histories. The black streakline connects present positions of the continuously released family, including release times between the sampled dots. After T=1 s, particles already present keep moving and new ones enter at the origin, so the later streakline is not a frozen record of the earlier one. Injection beginning only at τ=1 s would show just 0≤x≤1 m of the T=2 s curve. Both panels are diffusion-free analytical models, not experimental photographs.
Kline's contracting-channel demonstration switches from marking an element to continuous bubble production at a marking wire: the resulting trace is a streakline. The apparatus therefore changes the curve being displayed by changing the marking history, even with the same channel. A wire produces a family of traces; conceptually each fixed emitting location supplies its own streakline. Individual bubbles are markers rather than perfect fluid elements: Jean Hertzberg's teaching notes describe hydrogen production by electrolysis at a thin cathode wire and warn that larger bubbles have more buoyancy. [ref] [ref]
A dye version uses a small fixed injection port upstream in a transparent water channel, a dilute premix of dye with the channel water, illumination and a fixed optical camera. Start continuous injection at a recorded time τ0​ and take a short exposure at T: the visible filament approximates a streakline, not the accumulated pathline of one particle. Repeat with the same port and imaging geometry after changing the flow with time; compare the filament against local directions estimated from short displacements of sparse markers at T. Agreement in a steady flow and possible disagreement when the flow changes are the predictions being tested; no measured curves are claimed here. The protocol follows Hertzberg's advice to use small ports, little injected volume and a dilute premix with matched density and viscosity. Check for nozzle disturbance by reducing injection rate, for buoyancy by watching the premix in still water, and for diffusion by comparing filament widths at different ages. Keep exposure short enough to suppress motion blur. Dye concentration approximates a passive scalar only when it has negligible feedback on the velocity field; finite port width, diffusion and out-of-plane motion limit how literally a visible filament can be read as a geometrical streakline. [ref]

Fluid entrainment

Words: 493 Articles: 7
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Fluid entrainment is the incorporation of surrounding fluid into a moving current, jet, or plume. It increases volume flux while diluting transported momentum, buoyancy, or concentration.

Entrainment velocity (ue​)

Words: 67
Fluid entrainment OurBigBook.com
The mean speed, measured normal to a chosen plume or jet boundary, at which ambient fluid enters the turbulent region. The boundary and averaging convention must be specified: this speed is not the plume's axial velocity. In the Batchelor entrainment hypothesis for a rising Boussinesq plume, ue​=αw, where α is the dimensionless entrainment coefficient and w the characteristic axial speed. Multiplying by the boundary perimeter gives the entrained volume flux per axial length.

Together with potential energy of two-layer entrainment, this gives h˙=2CW​cD​uI3​/(g′h). This is an additional local power-transfer closure. The shaft power of a rotating lid is its torque times its prescribed angular speed and need not equal PI​. Geometric factors and a constant transfer fraction may be absorbed into the empirical coefficients only when explicitly assumed time-independent.

With depth z increasing downward, gravitational potential energy is −gS∫0H​ρ(z)zdz=E∗​+ρl​SBh/2, so its rate of increase is proportional to the rate of deepening. This includes homogenization throughout the upper layer, not merely lifting a thin parcel across the interface.

Natural ventilation

Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Natural ventilation exchanges indoor and outdoor fluid through openings using pressure differences created by buoyancy or wind.

Ventilation after a heating reduction (xs​=1−x​−λ)

Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
For an ideal two-layer natural ventilation transient following a heating change Q↦λQ, let V0​ and θ0​ be the initial flow and temperature excess, s=V0​t/(Ar​H), η=h/H, and x=η(1−θ/θ0​). The integrated buoyancy pressure gives V/V0​=1−x​, while heat balance gives xs​=1−x​−λ. A material interface satisfies ηs​=1−x​, so η=x+λs. For 0<λ<1, x increases toward 1−λ2 and ηs​≥λ, ensuring finite-time filling of the room. After filling, y=θ/θ0​ obeys ys​=λ−y3/2 and tends to λ2/3. This model assumes well-mixed individual layers, negligible wall heat capacity and a sharp advected interface.

Words: 200 Articles: 2
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
For a distributed heat source, a well-mixed interior with temperature excess θ gains temperature-volume flux H and loses ∣q∣θ by ventilation in either direction. With signed upward throughflow, q∣q∣=KA​(GT​θ±W), where GT​=gαT​Hb​ and W is wind pressure divided by mass density. The plus sign is assisting wind. Steady temperatures satisfy θ2(GT​θ+W)=H2/KA​ for assistance, or θ2∣GT​θ−W∣=H2/KA​ for opposition. Direction restrictions must be applied to roots.

Words: 136 Articles: 1
Well-mixed ventilation temperature balance OurBigBook.com
For 0<ε<2/(33​), the well-mixed ventilation temperature balance has one stable upward-flow temperature and two downward-flow temperatures. The heat-removal curve on the latter interval is KA​​θW−GT​θ​, maximal at 2W/(3GT​). Its lower-temperature root is stable and its higher-temperature root unstable. The two meet at a saddle-node bifurcation. The unstable root separates the basins of the stable wind-dominated and buoyancy-dominated states.
Ventilation switching under wind and heating changes
Words: 81
Opposing-wind ventilation bistability OurBigBook.com
Increasing wind or reducing heating both reduce the control parameter of opposing-wind ventilation bistability. However, wind moves the reversal threshold θw​=W/GT​, whereas heating does not. A sufficiently abrupt wind increase can place a hot upward-flow state in the cooler state's basin. Reducing positive heating at fixed wind cannot make an upward-flow state cross θw​, because its temperature time derivative there is positive. Slow variation follows a persistent stable branch; a fold destroys the cooler branch when wind is weakened or heat input increased.

Two equal openings carrying the same flux share the total pressure drop, so q2=Ae2​Δp/(2ρ). They do not share equal drops when an internal volume source makes their fluxes unequal. State the effective-area convention before comparing numerical factors in natural ventilation models.

Displacement ventilation supplies relatively cool air at low level and removes warmer air at high level. In the ideal two-layer model, buoyant plumes feed a warm upper layer above a sharp density interface while the supply occupies the lower layer.

Warm air above the doorway stores heat but adds no available head at its crest in this uniform-layer model.

The upper outflow carries both sources, so g2′​=(B1​+B2​)/Q, yielding the displayed ratio. Opening flow is driven by the integrated hydrostatic head g1′​(h2​−h1​)+g2′​(H−h2​). A plume crossing the lower interface has altered buoyancy relative to its new ambient and must be continued with nonzero incoming mass and momentum fluxes rather than reset as a zero-flux pure plume.

A source volume Q makes roof outflow exceed floor inflow by Q. At zero floor inflow, an entraining plume cannot support a steady cold lower layer; the warm layer reaches the floor. With reduced gravity g′=B/Q, the entire hydrostatic head drives roof discharge Q=Ae​g′H​. This gives the stated threshold. Equal splitting of pressure head is inappropriate at blocking. The same result in physical-area notation is Qc​=(2Cd2​Ageom2​BH)1/3.

Words: 100
Displacement ventilation OurBigBook.com
Consider entraining plumes supplied with total source volume flux S, a separate lower-layer ambient inflow L, and ceiling exhaust F=S+L. Write P(h)=S+E(h), where E(h) is total fluid entrainment from the lower layer. Volume conservation gives Ah˙=L−E(h). A steady positive lower layer therefore requires L=E(h)>0. If L=0 and E(h)>0 for every h>0, no positive steady displacement-ventilation interface height exists. In a shifted pure plume approximation Pi​(h)=λBi1/3​(h+zi​)5/3 matched to source flux Si​ at h=0, this follows immediately from Pi​(h)>Si​ for h>0. This is a statement about the ideal two-layer model, not a prohibition of all possible stratification in a real ventilated room.

A tall opening between fluids of different densities can support simultaneous inflow below a neutral pressure level and outflow above it. For a symmetric opening with a Boussinesq hydrostatic pressure difference and equal discharge coefficients, the neutral level lies at mid-height.

The neutral pressure level is the height at which indoor and outdoor hydrostatic pressures agree. Flow through an opening reverses direction across this level.

A stratified-room plume-exchange model balances the upward volume transported by a warm plume against downward transport by cold wall plumes. A global buoyancy balance relates the source flux to the buoyancy carried out through the vents.
